title: Embed token-split regression and autoscale misfire postmortem
creator: Maya Chen
description: Summary: On 2025-02-18 at ~06:30 UTC the embeddings + reranking pipeline experienced a simultaneous capacity drop and quality regression lasting ~7 hours. Root causes were a microscopic upstream tokenization change that increased token counts for ~14% of incoming documents and a misconfiguration in the Dedicated autoscaler policy that prevented rapid scale-up during the sustained token-length shift. The net effect: higher per-request GPU memory usage, queuing and throttle behavior, increased latencies, and degraded rerank quality for some customers using length-sensitive prompts. This postmortem documents timeline, impact, root cause analysis, mitigations performed during the incident, and long-term fixes.
impact: Between 2025-02-18 06:30 UTC and 2025-02-18 13:45 UTC: 12% of requests to /v1/embeddings and /v1/rerank experienced >2x latency spikes. Error rate (503/429) rose from baseline 0.6% to 6.9% at peak. 7 enterprise customers reported ranking score regressions on canonical evals (median NDCG drop of 0.07 on affected prompts). No data exfiltration. Estimated lost revenue exposure: one-day equivalent of 0.9% of monthly run-rate for Dedicated tenants affected.
timeline: 2025-02-18 06:20 UTC - Canary telemetry: small uptick in median token count for embeddings service seen in synthetic canary (not alerted).
2025-02-18 06:30 UTC - Customer pager hits: increased 5xx/429 errors reported by two Dedicated tenants. Ops on-call notified by Slack alert (latency SLO breach).
2025-02-18 06:45 UTC - Initial mitigation: route traffic off busiest GPU pool to fallback pool; short-term routing reduced error rate but increased latencies. Engineering begins investigation.

2025-02-18 07:10 UTC - Root trigger discovered: latest tokenizer library bump deployed three hours prior to incident in a subset of clients (new whitespace-splitting rule) increased average tokenization length for some document types (HTML snippets, markdown lists).

2025-02-18 07:25 UTC - Autoscaler audit: Dedicated autoscaler had a scale-up cooldown set to 20m and a per-pool max-burst flag disabled; policy incorrectly excluded memory pressure derived autoscaling signal. Scale attempts queued but not provisioned quickly enough.
2025-02-18 07:40 UTC - Emergency config change: reduce cooldown to 60s, enable burst provisioning; immediate scale up started.

2025-02-18 08:15 UTC - Hotfix deployed: temporarily pin tokenizer version for request-side library to prior behavior for Dedicated customers using the SDK; webhook created to notify embedded customers.
2025-02-18 10:00 UTC - Gradual roll-back: tokenizer change rolled back in upstream service; canaries validated reduced token counts.
2025-02-18 11:30 UTC - Observability: added token-count histogram to SLO dashboards and set alert for median token increase >10% over baseline.
2025-02-18 13:45 UTC - Incident declared resolved; follow-up actions assigned.
root_cause: Two-contributor failure: (1) a tokenizer update (lib-text-tokenize 2.7.0) changed the split behavior for certain punctuation/whitespace patterns, increasing token counts for a non-trivial fraction of documents; this caused higher per-request memory/compute. (2) The Dedicated autoscaler configuration did not include memory-pressure or token-count-derived signals for rapid scale-up and had an overly long cooldown, preventing quick provisioning. Independently tolerable; together they caused capacity starvation and emergent queuing and fallbacks that degraded latency and rerank quality.
detection: Initial detection via customer-reported errors and SLO alerts for latency. Pre-existing synthetic canaries had a small median token increase signal but the threshold was set too high. No specific alert was set for sudden tokenizer-driven token count changes.
mitigations: Routed traffic off the most affected GPU pool to fallback pools to immediately reduce errors (operational routing override).
Reduced Dedicated autoscaler cooldown from 20m to 60s and enabled burst provisioning flags to allow rapid scale up.
Pinned request-side tokenizer at previous major version for Dedicated SDKs and applied a server-side input normalization fallback to reduce token blowup for incoming payloads.
Informed affected customers via support channel and provided a temporary configuration knob to reject extremely large tokenized inputs with a clear 413 response and guidance.
Deployed rollback of tokenizer change in the internal ingestion pipeline and validated with canaries before re-enabling.
Added temporary increased GPU headroom on critical pools while autoscaler config stabilized.
long_term_fix: Add token-count as a first-class metric to autoscaler decision-making (include 95th/99th percentiles and memory-estimated token cost).
Create a lightweight pre-tokenize fast-path on the ingress layer that rejects or normalizes pathological inputs with better client-facing errors and telemetry.
Introduce library compatibility gating in SDKs: SDKs will pin tokenizer versions by default and surface opt-in flags for experimental tokenizer upgrades.
Revise autoscaler policy: include memory-pressure signals, reduce default cooldowns for burst scenarios, and add predictive rules for sudden token distribution shifts.
Improve canary thresholds and add an explicit alert for median token-count changes >10% within a 15-minute window.
Add a rerank-quality regression check that runs new embeddings through a small canonical eval set in pre-prod when tokenizer or model changes are deployed.

ENG-33129: Build ingress pre-tokenize fast-path and normalization (owner: Jorge Alvarez, due: 2025-03-07).
ENG-33130: SDK tokenizer-gating and opt-in flag (owner: Sara Li, due: 2025-03-21).
ENG-33131: Add canary alert and rerank-quality pre-prod eval (owner: Liam O'Connor, due: 2025-03-03).
ENG-33132: Autoscaler policy audit and defaults overhaul (owner: Helena Markov, due: 2025-04-01).
ENG-33133: Postmortem review with Customer Success and Product to update external communication templates (owner: Maya Chen, due: 2025-02-28).
notes: Lessons: small upstream library changes can have outsized production effects when combined with brittle autoscaler policies. Prioritize observability around input characteristics (token counts) as strongly as CPU/memory signals. Customer-facing SDKs should be conservative about opt-in tokenizer upgrades for Dedicated/Private deployments.
